title: Greetings and common expressions
summary: Pô and opô, greetings through the day, how are you, five ways to say excuse me, and everyday expressions
goals: Use pô, hô, opô and ohô to show respect, and know who does not use them
Greet people from morning to evening, politely and between equals
Ask and answer "how are you?" and recognise greetings that are really questions
Choose the right way to say excuse me
Use the everyday expressions and their shortened forms

sections.title: Pô and hô: polite forms of address

blocks.t: Besides the borrowed *Hi* and *Hello*, Tagalog greetings carry little words that show courtesy and respect. The most important are **pô** and **hô**. They mean roughly **sir** or **madam**, and they show the speaker's good manners and respect for the person spoken to.
Younger people and junior employees put **pô** or **hô** at the **start or end** of their greetings and answers when speaking to:

head: Who
Examples
rows: parents, older relatives, other senior individuals
people with honorific titles or authority, regardless of age
clergy, teachers, community leaders, employers, policemen
blocks.title: Use pô or hô when speaking to
Who does not use pô
items: An older person speaking to a younger one, such as a father talking to his son or daughter.
Equals, such as brothers and sisters or friends.

blocks.t: Saying yes
To a younger person or a friend, a short yes can be just **oo**. To an older person, you must use **opô** or **ohô**, the formal or polite versions of yes.

head: Speaking to
Yes
rows: a younger person or a peer
blocks.title: Familiar and polite yes
You can't overdo it
blocks.t: Foreigners and Tagalogs alike could never go wrong with an overuse of pô. It will only endear them to older or senior people.
Greetings usually start with **magandá**, which means *beautiful*. The complete greeting is **Magandá ang áraw**, often shortened to **Magandáng áraw**, which literally means *beautiful day*.

head: Greeting
Meaning
blocks.title: Polite greetings from morning to evening
Tanghálì
blocks.t: **Tanghálì** is *noon* or *midday*. It covers lunch time, from around 11 in the morning to 1 in the afternoon, when most Tagalog families prepare and have their lunch.
Between equals it is fine to drop pô: **Magandáng umága.** (Good morning.) **Magandáng hápon.** (Good afternoon.)
Even more polite: sa inyó and sa kanilá

Another polite way to greet people is to use the **plural**. Add **sa inyó** (*to you*, plural) or **sa kanilá** (*to them*) at the end. A greeting ending in sa kanilá still means *to you*, not *to them*. The plural shows that you recognise the person's seniority or authority. Equals use **sa iyó** (*to you*, singular).
Replying
Both older people and equals usually reply with **rin** or **namán**, which mean *too*. It shows they wish the greeter a good day as well.
**Kumustá** comes from the Spanish *como esta*. Use **Kumustá ka?** with a friend, a relative, or someone about your age. Older people also use it with younger people.

The word for *you* (one person) is **ikáw**. It becomes **ka** when it comes after the main word (Lessons 5 and 6 explain this). When greeting an elder or a superior, Tagalogs use the plurals **kayó** (*you*) and **silá** (*they*) instead of ka. Pô may be dropped if kayó or silá is used.

head: Say
Meaning
Who to
rows: a friend, a relative, someone your age, a younger person
blocks.title: Asking how someone is
Answering
items: Answers usually include **mabúti** (*fine*), **salámat** (*thank you*), and **rin** or **namán** (*too*).
Salámat is optional at the end, so pô can go with the first half of the answer.
It is never wrong to say pô again when salámat is kept.

blocks.title: Asking about the family
blocks.t: Tagalogs often ask about your family (parents, spouse, children and everyone else) when they meet, whatever their age. It shows the thoughtful nature of Filipinos, young and old alike.
Greetings that are really questions

Tagalogs also say *Where are you going?* or *Where have you been?* when they meet people they know. They are not really asking your plans. It is like the English *How is it going?*, just another way of saying hello.
The usual answer is **Diyán lámang (pô)**, which means *Just nearby (sir/madam)*. You can also name the place: **Sa Quezon City (pô)** means *I'm going to Quezon City* or *I've been to Quezon City*.

sections.title: Five ways to say excuse me

blocks.t: Tagalog has no exact word for *excuse me*. Instead there are **five** expressions, each for a different situation.

head: Say
Used when
rows: you apologise or ask to be excused, or you bump into someone by accident
you ask permission to pass through
you apologise for causing physical injury or emotional hurt
you warn people of something that may be offensive or distasteful
blocks.title: The five expressions

blocks.t: In real situations

head: Situation
What to say
Meaning
rows: Excuse me (sir/madam), I will leave now.
Stepping out of a meeting for a while
Excuse me (sir/madam), I will go out for a while.
Bumping into someone at a party or in a crowded mall
Two people talking are blocking a hallway
Voicing a request or opinion, or interrupting a speaker in a meeting
I beg your pardon… (literally: May I lose my courtesy?)
Asking directions from someone talking to another person
Mawaláng-gálang pô, paano pumuntá sa Ayala Avenue?
Excuse me, how do I get to Ayala Avenue?
You have deeply hurt someone, physically or emotionally
Warning people before unpleasant stories, photos or film
blocks.title: Which one, when
Can one replace another?
items: **Mawaláng-gálang pô** may be used for situations 1 and 2 (leaving or stepping out, and passing through), but not for a real hurt.
**Paumanhin pô** may mean *Sorry*, but it is too mild for physical or emotional injury. Use **Patawad pô** instead.
News reporters often say **Pasintabi pô** before showing gruesome film footage on television.

blocks.t: Tagalogs use these everyday expressions all the time. Many have **shortened forms** used in everyday speech, just as English uses *Let's* for *Let us*. Memorise them as whole phrases.
Sigúro: maybe or definitely
**Sigúro** can mean *maybe* or *definitely*. The meaning depends on the answer. Here are three answers to **Siguro ka?** (*Are you sure?*):

head: Answer
Meaning
rows: Yes, I am sure (or Yes, definitely).

blocks.title: Be respectful
blocks.t: Add **pô** to these expressions, or change **ka** into **kayó** or **silá**, whenever possible to show respect.

blocks.title: Mabúhay!
blocks.t: **Mabuhay** is the official greeting of Filipinos to foreign visitors. It is also used to show joy and pride on any occasion, such as an achievement in politics or sports, and to greet newlyweds: **Mabuhay ang bagong kasal!** (*May the newlyweds live long!*). **Maligáyang batì** now goes with birthday celebrations.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Pô and hô show respect to older people and to people in authority. Opô and ohô are the polite yes.
Magandáng + áraw, umága, tanghálì, hápon or gabí. Reply with rin or namán.
Kumustá ka? for friends; Kumustá pô kayó? or Kumustá silá? for elders.
Saán ka púpuntá? is just a friendly hello.
Five ways to say excuse me: Paumanhín, Pakiraán, Mawaláng-gálang, Patáwad, Pasintábi.

exercises.q: Who would you say pô to?
options: An older person or someone in authority
exercises.answer: An older person or someone in authority
exercises.explain: Pô shows respect to older people and to people with honorific titles or authority.

exercises.q: Does a father use pô when talking to his son?
exercises.explain: An older person does not use pô when talking to a younger person.

exercises.q: Do equals, such as siblings or friends, use pô with each other?
exercises.explain: Equals do not use the term.

exercises.q: How do you say "yes" to an older person?
exercises.explain: Opô or ohô are the formal, polite versions of yes.

exercises.q: Which word starts most Tagalog greetings?
exercises.explain: Magandá means beautiful. Magandáng áraw literally means beautiful day.

exercises.q: What is tanghálì?
exercises.explain: It covers lunch time, from around 11 am to 1 pm.

exercises.q: Someone says "Magandáng umága." What is a good reply?
exercises.explain: Namán (or rin) means too.

exercises.q: What does "sa kanilá" mean at the end of a greeting?
exercises.explain: In a greeting it still means to you. The plural shows respect.

exercises.q: How do you ask an elder "How are you?"
exercises.explain: Use the plural kayó (or silá) for elders and superiors.

exercises.q: When someone asks "Saán ka púpuntá?", they are usually…
exercises.explain: It is like the English How is it going?

exercises.q: What is the usual answer to "Saán ka nanggáling?"
exercises.explain: It means Just nearby.

exercises.q: You bump into somebody in a crowded mall. What do you say?
exercises.explain: Paumanhín pô is for bumping into someone by accident.

exercises.q: Two people talking are blocking the hallway. What do you say?
exercises.explain: Pakiraán pô means Please let me pass.

exercises.q: You want to interrupt a speaker in a meeting to make a comment. What do you say?
exercises.explain: It is used when one requests to be heard.

exercises.q: You have deeply hurt someone. What do you say?
exercises.explain: Paumanhin pô is too mild for physical or emotional injury.

exercises.q: A news reporter is about to show gruesome footage. What do they say?
exercises.explain: It warns people of something offensive.

exercises.q: Your mother calls you to dinner but you are still tidying your desk. What do you say?
exercises.explain: Sandalî lámang means Just a moment.

exercises.q: Your grandmother asks a question but you didn't understand it. What do you say?
exercises.explain: Anó pô? means What did you say, sir/madam?

exercises.q: Your 2-year-old nephew sings a whole song. What do you say?
exercises.explain: Magalíng means Outstanding! (literally: Skilled).

exercises.q: The town mayor greets you good afternoon. What do you reply?
exercises.explain: Repeat the greeting with too and pô.

exercises.q: What is the shortened form of "Táyo na"?
exercises.explain: Táyo na (Let's go) is shortened to Tena.

exercises.q: What does "Sigúro" mean on its own?
exercises.explain: Sigúro can mean maybe or definitely, depending on the answer.
Salámat means thank you.
Mabúti means fine.
Sáyang! means What a pity. What a loss.

recap: Pô and hô show respect to older people and anyone with authority. Opô and ohô are the polite yes; oo is for younger people and peers.
Greetings: Magandáng + áraw, umága, tanghálì, hápon or gabí (+ pô). Reply with rin or namán.
Sa inyó and sa kanilá at the end make a greeting even more polite.
Kumustá ka? for friends; Kumustá pô kayó? or Kumustá silá? for elders.
Saán ka púpuntá? and Saán ka nanggáling? are just hellos. Answer: Diyán lámang.
Five ways to say excuse me: Paumanhín, Pakiraán, Mawaláng-gálang, Patáwad, Pasintábi.
